findings.summary: The `always` restart policy is described as restarting a container even after a manual stop, but Docker ignores the policy for manually stopped containers until the daemon restarts.
findings.evidence: "`always` restarts on any exit, even after a manual stop" / "`unless-stopped` is like always, but respects a manual stop"
findings.fix: Write: "`always` restarts on any exit, and after a manual stop only when the daemon restarts or you start the container again. `unless-stopped` stays stopped even after a daemon restart."

findings.summary: The prune story is wrong for current Docker. Since Docker 23, `docker system prune --volumes` removes only anonymous volumes, so a named volume like `db` is not deleted.
findings.evidence: "Ran `docker system prune --volumes` with the DB container stopped" / "A volume no container uses counts as **unused**, so it was deleted"
findings.fix: Say that `docker volume prune -a` (or `--all`) removes unused named volumes, and that `docker system prune --volumes` removes only anonymous ones on Docker 23 and later. Or rewrite the mistake around `docker volume prune -a` or `docker volume rm`.

findings.summary: PID 1 without a SIGTERM handler ignores the signal rather than dying. The container is killed only when `docker stop` times out and sends SIGKILL.
findings.evidence: "So the app must handle SIGTERM itself, or it gets killed"
findings.fix: Write: "So the app must handle SIGTERM itself, or the signal is ignored and `docker stop` sends SIGKILL after the timeout."

findings.summary: The Containers page relies on shell-form CMD, and on `-p`, which are only taught on later pages.
findings.evidence: "Shell-form CMD hides the app from SIGTERM" and the example "docker run -d --name web \\ -p 8080:80" appear here. Shell vs exec form is taught on the Dockerfile page (7), and `-p` publishing on the Networking page (12).
findings.fix: Add one short clause on this page saying shell form wraps the app in `sh -c`, so it never sees SIGTERM. Add a short note that `-p host:container` publishes a port and that Networking covers it. Or drop the shell-form bullet here and keep it on the Dockerfile page.

findings.summary: The Security page uses "capabilities" and "setuid" as known terms without defining them, so the `--cap-drop` advice rests on an undefined concept.
findings.evidence: "`--cap-drop ALL`, then add back only what is needed; defaults are too broad" and "`--security-opt no-new-privileges` blocks setuid escalation". The table row "Capabilities | ALL dropped | all granted" never says what a capability is.
findings.fix: Add a clause defining capabilities as fine-grained slices of root power, for example NET_BIND_SERVICE allows binding ports below 1024. Add a clause saying setuid binaries run with their owner's privileges.

findings.summary: Three bullets on the Debugging page appear after the flowchart with no heading. They reference build and disk-cleanup tooling that is only introduced on the next page.
findings.evidence: "Plain progress prints every build step's output" and "`prune` cleans stopped containers, dangling images, networks". The commands `--progress=plain` and `docker system prune` first appear on page 19.
findings.fix: Move these bullets to page 19 under the build-failure and disk-full material. Or name the commands in full here: `docker build --progress=plain --no-cache` and `docker system prune`.

findings.summary: The Production page says to set "limits and requests", but requests is a Kubernetes-only term. It was never introduced, and the page gives no example.
findings.evidence: "Set memory and CPU ==limits and requests== on every container". Page 5 only taught limits such as `--memory`, and the page's code example shows no request.
findings.fix: Say "limits (and, in Kubernetes, requests, the amount reserved for scheduling)". Or drop "requests" and reuse the `--memory`/`--cpus` flags from the Containers page.
